section.title: The ooSQLValue Class
section.para: The ooSQLValue class reads the arguments of the user defined SQL functions and aggregates written in Rexx, which are registered with the createFunction method of the ooSQLiteConnection class. Its methods are class methods: there are no ooSQLValue objects. Each method takes one of the values that the callback method receives, and returns it in a Rexx form: as a number, a string, or a blob, or its datatype.
The ooSQLResult class sets the result of those functions. The oosqlValue routines, such as oosqlValueText, do the same as the methods of this class in the classic interface.

section.title: Method Table
section.para: The following table provides links to the documentation of the methods used in reading the arguments of a user defined SQL function with the ooSQLValue class.

section.title: &changed11;blob (Class method)
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a blob.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.

A string with the bytes of the value, including any NUL characters. A value that is not a blob is converted: text is returned as is, and a number as its text representation. An empty blob returns the empty string, and a NULL value returns the .nil object.

What is said here applies to all the methods of the ooSQLValue class. They are used inside the callback methods of the functions and aggregates defined with createFunction. SQLite passes each argument of the SQL function to the method as a Pointer object, the sqlValue: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, and the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. The methods of the ooSQLValue class return the value in the form that is asked for, converting it if needed. type tells which type the value has. They are class methods: they are sent to the class, as in .ooSQLValue~text(value).

A sqlValue is only valid during the invocation of the method that received it. &changed11;A Pointer that is not a value, or a value that is no longer valid, raises a syntax error, 88.900: see Handles. Before ooSQLite 1.1 it could crash the interpreter.
int, int64, double, text, and blob return .nil for a NULL value. Use type to test for NULL before asking for the value.
The functionality of the blob method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_blob API.
The oosqlValueBlob routine does the same in the classic interface.
Before ooSQLite 1.1, this method returned the empty string for NULL as well as for an empty blob.

This example defines a describe function that tells an empty blob from NULL, and displays the bytes of any other value:
rc = db~createFunction("describe", .Values~new, 1, "describe") sql = "SELECT describe(x'CAFE') AS a, describe(x'') AS b, describe(NULL) AS" - "c, describe('ab') AS d;" rows = db~exec(sql, .true) say rows[1]['A'] '/' rows[1]['B'] '/' rows[1]['C'] '/' rows[1]['D'] /* Output: 2 byte(s): CAFE / empty / NULL / 2 byte(s): 6162 */
::class Values ::method describe use arg db, context, userData, value data = .ooSQLValue~blob(value) select when data == .nil then text = 'NULL' when data == '' then text = 'empty' otherwise text = .ooSQLValue~bytes(value) 'byte(s):' data~c2x end .ooSQLResult~text(context, text) return 0

section.title: bytes (Class method)
section.para: Returns the size in bytes of one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.
The size of a blob, or of the UTF-8 text of any other value: the number 3.9 has 3 bytes. A NULL value has 0 bytes.

The size is that of the value as it is when the method is invoked: numericType can convert a text to a number, and then its size changes. See the remarks of blob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the bytes method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_bytes API.
The oosqlValueBytes routine does the same in the classic interface.
See the example of blob.

section.title: &changed11;double (Class method)
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a floating point number.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.

The value as a number, with all its precision: the shortest number, of up to 17 significant digits, that is converted back to the same floating point value. Text that starts with a number is converted to that number; a blob, and text that does not start with a number, return 0. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.

A Rexx program computes with 9 digits unless it sets NUMERIC DIGITS: the number keeps its precision, but an arithmetic operation on it is rounded to the current setting. See the remarks of blob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the double method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_double API.
The oosqlValueDouble routine does the same in the classic interface.
Before ooSQLite 1.1, the number was returned with 9 significant digits only: 3.141592653589793 was returned as 3.14159265.

This example defines a function that returns, as text, the number that the Rexx method receives:
rc = db~createFunction("asSeenByRexx", .Numbers~new, 1, "asSeenByRexx") sql = "SELECT asSeenByRexx(pi()) AS a, asSeenByRexx(0.1) AS b," - "asSeenByRexx('2.50') AS c;" rows = db~exec(sql, .true) say rows[1]['A'] rows[1]['B'] rows[1]['C'] /* Output: 3.141592653589793 0.1 2.5 */
::class Numbers ::method asSeenByRexx use arg db, context, userData, value .ooSQLResult~text(context, .ooSQLValue~double(value)) return 0

section.title: int (Class method)
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a 32-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.

The value as a whole number. A floating point value is truncated, so 3.9 is 3, and text that starts with a number is converted to that number; a blob, and text that does not start with a number, return 0. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.

When the value does not fit in 32 bits, only its lower 32 bits are returned, and the result is not meaningful: use int64 for values that can be that large. See the remarks of blob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the int method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_int API.
The oosqlValueInt routine does the same in the classic interface.
See the examples of int64 and zeroBlob.

section.title: int64 (Class method)
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a 64-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.
The value as a whole number, converted as int does. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.

The method that computes with the value may need a higher NUMERIC DIGITS setting than the default of 9, as the example does. See the remarks of blob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the int64 method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_int64 API.
The oosqlValueInt64 routine does the same in the classic interface.

This example defines a half function, which works with numbers that do not fit in 32 bits:
rc = db~createFunction("half", .Numbers~new, 1, "half") sql = "SELECT half(9000000000) AS a, half(7) AS b, half('41') AS c," - "quote(half(NULL)) AS d;" rows = db~exec(sql, .true) say rows[1]['A'] rows[1]['B'] rows[1]['C'] rows[1]['D'] /* Output: 4500000000 3 20 NULL */
::class Numbers ::method half use arg db, context, userData, value numeric digits 19 n = .ooSQLValue~int64(value) if n == .nil then .ooSQLResult~null(context) else .ooSQLResult~int64(context, n % 2) return 0

section.title: numericType (Class method)
section.para: Returns the datatype of one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function, after converting a text that looks like a number to that number.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.
One of the Fundamental Datatype constants, as type returns. For a text that is a well formed number, possibly with spaces around it, the type is INTEGER or FLOAT instead of TEXT.

The conversion is done in place: once this method has converted a text, the value is that number, for type, text, bytes, and the other methods. Use type first when the original type matters. A text that only starts with a number, such as '12abc', is not converted. See the remarks of blob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the numericType method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_numeric_type API.
The oosqlValueNumericType routine does the same in the classic interface.

This example displays, for some texts, the type before the conversion, the type that numericType returns, and the type after it:
rc = db~createFunction("kinds", .Values~new, 1, "kinds") rows = db~exec("SELECT kinds('12') AS a, kinds(' 3.5 ') AS b, kinds('12abc') AS c;", .true) say rows[1]['A'] '/' rows[1]['B'] '/' rows[1]['C'] /* Output: TEXT INTEGER INTEGER / TEXT FLOAT FLOAT / TEXT TEXT TEXT */
::class Values ::method kinds use arg db, context, userData, value names = .array~of('INTEGER', 'FLOAT', 'TEXT', 'BLOB', 'NULL') before = names[.ooSQLValue~type(value)] numeric = names[.ooSQLValue~numericType(value)] after = names[.ooSQLValue~type(value)] .ooSQLResult~text(context, before numeric after) return 0

section.title: text (Class method)
section.para: Returns one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function as a string.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.

The value as a string: text as is, and a number as its text representation. For a blob, the bytes before its first NUL character are returned: use blob for all of them. For a NULL value, the .nil object is returned.
This is the method used most to read the arguments of a function, because any value can be represented as a string. See the remarks of blob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the text method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_text API.
The oosqlValueText routine does the same in the classic interface.
See the examples of text and int.

section.title: type (Class method)
section.para: Returns the datatype of one of the values passed to a user defined SQL function.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlValue [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the callback method: the fourth and following arguments of the method of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step method of an aggregate. See the remarks of blob.
One of the Fundamental Datatype constants: INTEGER, FLOAT, TEXT, BLOB, or SQLNULL.

SQLite is dynamically typed: the same function can get values of different types in different invocations, whatever the declared types of the columns they come from. numericType also tells whether a text looks like a number. See the remarks of blob for where the values come from, and when they are valid.
The functionality of the type method is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_value_type API.
The oosqlValueType routine does the same in the classic interface.

This example defines a kind function that returns the name of the type of its argument:
rc = db~createFunction("kind", .Values~new, 1, "kind") sql = "SELECT kind(12) AS a, kind(1.5) AS b, kind('12') AS c, kind(x'00') AS" - "d, kind(NULL) AS e;" rows = db~exec(sql, .true) say rows[1]['A'] rows[1]['B'] rows[1]['C'] rows[1]['D'] rows[1]['E'] /* Output: INTEGER FLOAT TEXT BLOB NULL */
::class Values ::method kind use arg db, context, userData, value names = .array~of('INTEGER', 'FLOAT', 'TEXT', 'BLOB', 'NULL') .ooSQLResult~text(context, names[.ooSQLValue~type(value)]) return 0
